title: Hillel and the cry in the city
carry: bitachon: the hands work, the heart trusts God

cards: Hillel the elder is walking home from a journey. Near the city, he hears a cry, someone screaming behind the walls. A mind can run straight home at a moment like that.
Is it my street? My door? The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, tells what Hillel said instead: he was confident the cry was not coming from his house.
He wasn't predicting the news. He had no way to know. Something in him was settled before he knew anything at all.

teach.b: Bitachon. Trust in God. Turn it four ways.
First, the verse. The Talmud reads Hillel's calm through a psalm: the one who trusts in the LORD is not afraid of evil tidings, because the heart is steady. Trust first, steadiness after.
Bitachon is not a guarantee that nothing hard will happen. Jewish thinkers describe it in more than one way. Some teach it as confidence that God will bring good.
Others teach it as confidence that whatever comes, a person is held, even when the news is bad. Both loosen worry's grip without pretending the world is safe. Third, the manna.
In the wilderness, Exodus tells, bread came down each morning, and the people were told to gather only the day's portion. What was saved for the next day spoiled.
Some teachers draw bitachon from that scene: today's portion today. Fourth, the hands still work.
Bahya ibn Paquda, whom this path met earlier, gives a whole section of Duties of the Heart to trust, and he doesn't tell anyone to stop working.
He describes a person who does their part with their hands and lets go of the outcome in their heart.

teach.h: CAST THY BURDEN UPON THE LORD.
teach.b: The Psalms put the letting go plainly: Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and He will sustain thee. And trust keeps yesterday's truth company: you can look straight at a hard fact and not be owned by it.

how: Some Jews study the Gate of Trust in Bahya ibn Paquda's Duties of the Heart, and some recite the manna passage from Exodus as part of their daily prayers as a reminder of trust.

o: trust that steadies the heart before the news comes
worry that braces you for the worst news
certainty that nothing bad will ever happen

p: confident the cry was not from his house

s: bitachon means nothing bad will happen
the tradition describes trust that holds even when the news is hard; it is not a guarantee.
Bahya ibn Paquda taught that trust means stop working

games.q: you're Hillel, walking home. you hear a cry from inside the city. what do you say?
o: run home, sure it's your family.
say you're confident it isn't from your house.
turn around and leave the city.
games.why: the Talmud says Hillel was confident the cry was not from his house, and reads his calm through the psalm about not fearing evil tidings.

practice: Let one worry come forward and name it plainly. Split it in two: the part in your hands today, a call, a form, a conversation, and the part no amount of thinking will move tonight.
If you pray, set that second part down with the psalm's words, cast thy burden upon the LORD; if not, picture it on a table, still in sight, out of your hands.

wordCard.voice: Bitachon. Trust in God: doing your part with your hands and letting the outcome go from your heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: trust, reliance, especially trust in God.

carryVoice: Your line: bitachon: the hands work, the heart trusts God. Like Hillel, settled before the news came. Until tomorrow.
